articles.title: Federal Grand Jury Probe Into Alaska’s ‘Decoy Dan’ Senate Candidacy Widens
articles.subtitle: Prosecutors have issued scores of subpoenas and target letters as Alaska counts ballots; those named deny wrongdoing and no charges have been announced
articles.excerpt: Federal prosecutors have reportedly issued more than 100 subpoenas and at least 20 target and preservation letters in a criminal investigation into how a second “Dan Sullivan” reached Alaska’s U.S. Senate ballot, as the race is still being counted.

toc.text: How the second Dan Sullivan reached the ballot
State inquiry and open legal questions

content.text: Federal prosecutors have widened a criminal investigation into how a second candidate named Dan Sullivan came to appear on Alaska’s U.S. Senate ballot, issuing scores of grand jury subpoenas and sending target and preservation letters to political operatives and lawyers, according to reporting by ABC News and Fox News. No charges have been announced, and the people and groups named in the reporting have denied wrongdoing.

The investigation is unfolding while Alaska is still counting ballots from the Nov. 3 general election. As of Monday afternoon, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 2,517 votes, Newsweek reported. Retired Petersburg teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is listed on the ballot with no party affiliation and is widely nicknamed “Decoy Dan,” received 3,651 votes, or 1.7 percent, more than the gap between the two leading candidates.
What federal prosecutors are doing

ABC News reported on Nov. 3, citing sources, that a federal grand jury in Alaska is examining possible conspiracy and donor-fraud offenses and that prosecutors are issuing more than 100 subpoenas. Fox News, also citing sources, put the total at more than 120 since the investigation began in July, including more than 30 in a single 24-hour period after The New York Times published its report in late October.

Both outlets reported that at least 20 target and preservation letters have been sent. A target letter tells the recipient they are under investigation, while a preservation letter asks them to keep communications and documents; neither means charges will follow. ABC described the use of target letters at this stage as unusually early. Citing the Times, Fox reported that letters went to Marc Elias, whose Elias Law Group represents Peltola’s campaign, and to an official at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC).

Separately, CNN reported, as relayed by The Jerusalem Post on Nov. 7, that Gerald Heikes, a long-shot Republican candidate in the race, was subpoenaed to appear before the grand jury and to produce records about political groups and other candidates, along with communications involving Peltola’s campaign, several political action committees and operatives tied to them. The subpoena was reportedly signed by a senior official in the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division in Washington. Heikes told CNN he was not recruited and “just took a chance.”

The Associated Press reported that FBI agents have also contacted donors to Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., some of whom said they were asked whether they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting. U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters at a news conference before Election Day that he was not making assumptions about whether a crime had been committed, according to Fox News. The Justice Department has declined to comment on the ongoing investigation. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News Digital there is a “FRAUD on the ballot.”
How the second Dan Sullivan reached the ballot

Dan J. Sullivan entered the race in June and finished in the top four in the August primary with about 2.5 percent of the vote, which qualified him for the general election, the AP reported. He appears on the ballot as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party listed, while the incumbent is identified as a Republican. State election officials had earlier tried to keep him off the ballot, but state courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected a Republican-backed effort to remove him.

On Oct. 28, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign had tried to get a second Sullivan onto the ballot to confuse voters. According to the AP’s account of the report, the Times reviewed text messages among campaign members about recruiting people with the Sullivan name, reported that DSCC staffers were part of some of the text exchanges, and drew in part on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August and reportedly tried to retract her comments.
Denials and responses

Peltola’s campaign said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign,” and the DSCC said it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” Peltola has denied any knowledge of attempts to recruit other candidates. Dan J. Sullivan said in June that he had no contact with her campaign (“Zero, none, zilch”), and Newsweek reported on Nov. 10 that he continues to deny coordinating with it.

Elias said, according to ABC News, that he “will not be intimidated by a sham investigation” and accused the administration of weaponizing the Justice Department against political opponents. Sen. Sullivan’s campaign said Alaskans “deserve the truth,” and Sullivan told CNN he expects to “lose a lot of votes to that trickery.”
The court fight over certification

Less than two weeks before Election Day, the Justice Department sued in federal court to block Alaska from certifying the Senate result if Sen. Sullivan lost, asking for a review of whether votes cast for the namesake were meant for the incumbent. President Trump has said he ordered the suit. On Nov. 1, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed it, calling the requested relief infeasible and writing that the government “provides no workable plan” for separating ballots while protecting ballot secrecy. She also cited the Constitution’s grant of election authority to the states and the Purcell principle, which discourages federal courts from changing election rules close to an election.

The Justice Department said the ruling rested on procedural grounds and did not dispute its claim that the namesake ran as a decoy. It appealed the same day, and Newsweek reported that briefing is not due until several weeks after Alaska plans to certify its results. Peltola’s campaign, the DSCC, Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and two voters represented by the ACLU had intervened on the state’s side.
State inquiry and open legal questions

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who leaves office next month, has ordered a state investigation. In a Nov. 8 interview on WABC radio’s The Cats Roundtable, he said investigators are examining whether any wrongdoing occurred, “especially anything that might resemble perjury,” Newsweek reported. His office did not respond to the outlet’s request for comment.

It is unclear whether recruiting a ballot-name candidate violates any criminal law. Newsweek reported that ballot stacking is not illegal at the federal level and quoted Florida State University law professor Michael Morley as calling the Justice Department’s lawsuit “completely meritless.” Scott Kendall, the Anchorage attorney who wrote the state’s 2020 ranked-choice voting measure, says the system neutralizes spoiler candidates and that “Decoy Dan” is unlikely to change the outcome, while the group Repeal Now says some voters picked the wrong Dan Sullivan or failed to rank candidates.
What happens next

No candidate is expected to reach 50 percent, so a ranked-choice tabulation is likely on Nov. 18. If current standings hold, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. would be the first candidate eliminated and his voters’ next choices would be redistributed. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive through Nov. 13, overseas ballots through Nov. 18, and certification is scheduled for Nov. 25.

The grand jury investigation and the Justice Department’s appeal both continue. The allegations in the Times report and the department’s claims about voter confusion have not been tested in court, and a subpoena or target letter is not a charge. This report will be updated as the count and the investigations develop.

articles.title: Murder Investigation Underway After Woman Found Dead in Norfolk
articles.subtitle: A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman was found dead at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham
articles.excerpt: A murder investigation has been launched in Dersingham, Norfolk, after a woman in her 40s was found dead at a Fern Hill property. A man in his 40s has been arrested.

toc.text: Man Held on Suspicion of Murder
Inspection of the Dead Body Anticipated to Provide More Evidence
Investigation Continues - Police Appeal for Information - PMQ

content.text: A murder investigation has been launched in Norfolk after a woman in her 40s was discovered dead at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, in the early hours of Sunday, October 4. The ambulance service called police to the address shortly after 2.20am and the woman was pronounced dead after officers arrived.

A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder and is being questioned at King's Lynn Police Investigation Center. Detectives are still trying to piece together how the woman died and he is in custody.

Norfolk Constabulary said detectives from the Norfolk and Suffolk Major Investigation Team are dealing with the case. Officers are continuing inquiries, and there is still a police cordon at the property. The woman's death is being investigated, and a post-mortem examination is being carried out by the Home Office to establish the cause and circumstances.
Woman Dies at Dersingham Home

Emergency services were called to a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham just after 2.20am on Sunday after the ambulance service contacted police. Police officers who attended the address found a woman, in her 40s, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

The incident has led to a major investigation by Norfolk Constabulary and detectives from the Norfolk and Suffolk Major Investigation Team are now investigating what happened at the property. Police have not released the woman's identity publicly and details surrounding the circumstances of her death are limited as the investigation is in its early stages.

Norfolk Constabulary said officers attended the property and found the woman, prompting the investigation. A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder and taken to the King's Lynn Police Investigation Center for questioning, the force confirmed. Detectives are still investigating, and he is still in custody.

The Independent and Sky News also said the police cordon was still in place around the property, with officers continuing to work at the scene. The cordon means investigators are still at the scene looking for evidence that could help them establish what happened before emergency services arrived.

Police have yet to release any further details about the relationship between the woman and the arrested man, nor have they publicly established a motive. As the inquiry progresses, investigators are expected to consider evidence from the property, witness information, and the results of forensic examinations.
Man Held on Suspicion of Murder

A man in his 40s has been arrested in connection with the death and is being questioned in police custody. Police have not released details of what led to the arrest, but officers attended the Fern Hill property and made the arrest.

The suspect was taken to the King's Lynn Police Investigation Center where he is being interviewed by detectives as part of the murder inquiry. He remains in custody and detectives from the Norfolk and Suffolk Major Investigation Team are leading the investigation, Norfolk Constabulary said in a statement.

Police have not released the man's name publicly and have not released any details of any other potential charges beyond the current suspicion of murder. Arrest on suspicion of murder does not mean that someone has been charged or convicted of a crime. Detectives will have to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death before deciding what action to take.

The investigation is in its infancy. Detective Inspector Alix Wright, from the Norfolk and Suffolk Major Investigation Team, said detectives were trying to establish the exact circumstances surrounding the woman's death, and appealed for anyone with relevant information to contact police.

The arrested man is being questioned as part of a wider investigation, which includes work at the property and attempts to trace potential witnesses. Police will probably check all available evidence before deciding what to do next in the case.
Inspection of the Dead Body Anticipated to Provide More Evidence

The Home Office is carrying out a post-mortem examination as part of its investigation into the woman's death. For detectives, the examination is an important step in trying to determine the cause and manner of death, and possibly in providing evidence relevant to the larger investigation.

A post-mortem examination by the Home Office was to be held on Monday, October 5, Norfolk Constabulary said. Sky News and The Independent also reported that the examination would be held while investigators continued their work at the scene.

The findings could aid investigators in determining whether injuries caused the death or some other cause and could affect the direction of the investigation. But police have not yet released details on the nature of the woman's death and detectives have warned that the investigation is still in its early stages.

Officers remain working at the property in Fern Hill, and a police cordon is in place. These sorts of restrictions enable the investigator to preserve possible evidence and to do a thorough search of the scene. Detectives may also speak to people who live nearby or who may have been in the area when emergency services were called.

Police haven't said how long the cordon will be in place. The investigation is expected to develop as forensic examinations; witness accounts and questioning give detectives a clearer picture of the events.

Authorities have urged the public to hold off on speculation about the circumstances of the death until investigators can figure out the facts. For now, the post-mortem findings and other evidence gathered during the inquiry could be important in determining what happens next with the case.
Investigation Continues - Police Appeal for Information - PMQ

Detectives are appealing for anyone with information that could assist with the investigation to come forward. Detective Inspector Alix Wright said the inquiry was at a very early stage and appealed for anyone who thought they could help to give information to police.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information should contact Norfolk Constabulary, quoting incident number 27 of Sunday, October 4, 2026. Information can be given by calling 101 or the Norfolk Police website.

Detectives are trying to build up a picture of the events leading up to the woman's death and the appeal is part of that investigation. Information from residents, witnesses or anyone who may have seen or heard anything unusual could assist investigators in building a clearer picture of what occurred at the property.

So far, the authorities have released only a little information about the circumstances of the death. Police have confirmed the woman was in her 40s. She was found at a property in Fern Hill and a man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder. Further details are expected to emerge as detectives continue with their inquiries.

The investigation indicates that police need the facts before they jump to conclusions about what happened. The post-mortem examination, forensic work, witness statements and the questioning of the arrested man are all expected to be considered as part of the evidence by detectives.

Police are continuing to investigate the murder and are asking members of the public who may have information to contact them directly rather than speculate in public about the case. The investigation is continuing.

keyTakeaways: A second prosecutor has resigned from the DOJ grand-conspiracy investigation.
The probe seeks to link prior Trump-related cases into a broader alleged plot.
Personnel turmoil has slowed progress and raised questions about the theory's strength.
articles.whyItMatters: High-level turnover inside a politically sensitive investigation affects both its credibility and the likelihood of any charges before or after the midterms.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Second prosecutor resigns from Justice Department 'grand conspiracy' probe
articles.subtitle: The departure adds to turmoil in an investigation that has sought to link prior cases against Trump into a broader plot
articles.excerpt: A second prosecutor has left the Justice Department investigation into whether former officials conspired against President Trump, people familiar with the matter said, underscoring continued upheaval in a probe that has moved in fits and starts.

content.text: A lawyer who previously backed false claims about the 2020 election has resigned from a Justice Department investigation examining whether former government officials conspired against President Trump, a person familiar with the matter said.

The departure of Kurt Olsen is the second high-profile exit from the so-called grand-conspiracy probe and comes weeks before the midterm elections. The investigation has pursued an expansive theory that multiple prior inquiries into Trump formed part of a coordinated effort to damage his political prospects.
The resignation

Olsen's exit follows the abrupt resignation earlier this month of a lead prosecutor on the same team. People familiar with the internal discussions said disagreements over the strength of the evidence and the proper scope of subpoenas contributed to the turnover.
The Justice Department has not publicly detailed the reasons for either resignation. A spokesperson declined to comment on personnel matters.
Scope of the probe

Investigators have focused on several major prior cases, including the inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 election and the classified-documents case centered on Mar-a-Lago. They have sought testimony from officials involved in those probes in search of evidence of an unlawful conspiracy to deprive Trump of his rights.
Defense lawyers for some of the witnesses have argued that the theory is poorly defined and that their clients' prior work was properly predicated on available evidence at the time.
Earlier setbacks

The probe has faced repeated personnel changes. In the spring, a lead national-security prosecutor was replaced after raising questions about the strength of a related false-statements investigation. Career lawyers have privately expressed concern that the expansive theory risks overreach.

Congressional oversight committees are expected to seek briefings on the status of the investigation after the midterms. For now, the second resignation leaves the team thinner and the timeline for any charging decisions less certain.

keyTakeaways: A hacking group claimed it stole sensitive FBI personnel data.
The compromise appears tied to a jobs-related system rather than core investigative networks.
The FBI has publicly vowed to pursue the attackers and is assessing employee risk.
articles.whyItMatters: Personnel data exposure can endanger agents and staff and reveals weaknesses in systems that sit outside the bureau's most hardened networks.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: FBI scrambling after breach exposes personnel data, officials say
articles.subtitle: Hackers claimed to have stolen sensitive information on bureau employees; the FBI vowed to pursue the group
articles.excerpt: A major data breach has left the FBI working to determine how much personnel information was taken, after a hacking group claimed it obtained sensitive data on bureau employees from a jobs-related system.

content.text: The FBI is investigating a breach of a personnel-related system after a well-known hacking group claimed it stole sensitive data on bureau employees, according to officials and public statements from the group.

In an internal memo described by people familiar with it, the bureau said it believed the intruders may have obtained information covering a large share of its workforce. The precise categories of data and the number of affected employees remain under assessment.
What is known

The compromise appears to have involved a jobs or applicant-related website rather than the FBI's core investigative networks. Even so, personnel records can include home addresses, contact information and other details that raise safety concerns for agents and staff.

Brett Leatherman, a senior cyber official at the FBI, released a video statement saying the bureau knows how to find the perpetrators and will pursue them. The statement did not disclose the full scope of the loss.
The hacking group

The group known as ShinyHunters has a track record of stealing large volumes of personal data and offering it for sale. Security researchers have linked the group to multiple high-profile breaches in recent years across technology and government-adjacent targets.

Attribution in cyber cases is often provisional in the early days. The FBI has not publicly confirmed every claim made by the group, but it has treated the incident as a serious personnel-security event.
Response and risks

Employees have been advised to monitor for phishing and physical-security risks. The bureau is working with partner agencies to assess whether any of the exposed data has appeared on criminal markets.
Lawmakers who oversee the FBI said they expect a classified briefing on the breach and on steps to harden personnel systems that sit outside the main investigative infrastructure.

keyTakeaways: The FTC and more than 20 states sued Amazon over advertising practices.
The complaint alleges overcharging and limited competition for sellers.
Amazon is expected to contest the claims in court.
articles.whyItMatters: Advertising is a major profit center for large platforms; a successful case could change how search and sponsored results work for millions of sellers.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: FTC and states sue Amazon over advertising practices
articles.subtitle: The complaint alleges the company overcharged advertisers and limited competition on its platform
articles.excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission and more than 20 states filed a lawsuit accusing Amazon of deceptive advertising practices that allegedly overcharged sellers and advertisers by billions of dollars.

content.text: The Federal Trade Commission, joined by more than 20 state attorneys general, filed a lawsuit accusing Amazon of advertising practices that allegedly overcharged advertisers and distorted competition on its marketplace.

The complaint claims Amazon used its control of search placement and sponsored-product tools to extract higher fees while limiting the ability of sellers to reach customers through independent channels.
The allegations

According to the suit, Amazon's advertising systems favored higher-paying sponsored placements in ways that were not adequately disclosed, and the company used its data advantage to steer shoppers toward results that maximized its own ad revenue.
States joining the case argued that small and mid-size sellers bore the cost through rising advertising budgets that did not reliably improve organic visibility.
Amazon's response

Amazon has denied the core allegations in prior related matters and is expected to contest the new complaint vigorously. The company has long argued that its advertising tools are optional, transparent and beneficial to sellers who choose to use them.
A company spokesperson said Amazon looks forward to showing that its practices comply with the law and that advertisers retain control over their spending.
What the case could mean

If successful, the suit could force changes to how sponsored products appear in search results and how fees are calculated. Remedies under discussion in antitrust circles include stronger disclosure rules and limits on self-preferencing.
The case adds to a broader wave of federal and state actions targeting large platform companies over advertising, search and marketplace power.

keyTakeaways: House Republicans are investigating a DEA tactic tied to fentanyl cases.
Critics say delayed seizures may have increased short-term street supply.
The DEA has defended controlled-delivery methods as necessary to target networks.
articles.whyItMatters: Fentanyl remains the leading driver of overdose deaths; any enforcement choice that trades short-term seizures for longer cases draws intense scrutiny.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: House Republicans open inquiry into DEA tactic tied to fentanyl trafficking
articles.subtitle: Lawmakers say a controversial enforcement approach may have allowed more of the drug onto U.S. streets
articles.excerpt: House Republicans launched an investigation into a Drug Enforcement Administration tactic that critics say permitted large volumes of fentanyl to reach the United States while agents pursued longer-term cases.

content.text: House Republicans have opened an investigation into a Drug Enforcement Administration approach that, according to critics, allowed significant quantities of fentanyl to move into the United States while agents built longer-running cases against trafficking networks.
The inquiry follows reporting and internal complaints that some controlled deliveries and delayed interdictions were authorized in ways that increased short-term street supply.
The tactic under scrutiny

Investigators are examining whether supervisors approved operations in which known shipments were monitored rather than immediately seized, with the goal of identifying higher-level organizers. Similar techniques are used in other drug investigations, but the lethality of fentanyl has raised the stakes of any delay.
Documents requested by the committee include after-action reports, risk assessments and communications between field offices and headquarters about specific operations.
Congressional concerns

Members of the House Oversight and Judiciary panels said the public deserves to know whether enforcement choices contributed to overdose deaths. They have asked the DEA for a full accounting of the policy and of any internal dissent.
Democratic members have cautioned against second-guessing complex investigations without a complete record, while agreeing that fentanyl interdiction standards should be transparent.
Agency position

The DEA has previously defended controlled-delivery techniques as essential to dismantling supply chains rather than merely seizing individual loads. The agency has not publicly detailed the specific operations under review.
A formal response to the committee's document requests is expected in the coming weeks.

articles.whyItMatters: The Secret Service's handling of sensitive information is central to presidential security and to public confidence in the agency.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Three Secret Service officials under investigation for potential misconduct
articles.subtitle: The internal review focuses on the agency's communications office amid broader scrutiny of security and leaks
articles.excerpt: The Secret Service's Office of Professional Responsibility is investigating three employees, including senior communications staff, for potential misconduct, according to people familiar with the matter.

content.text: Three Secret Service employees are under internal investigation for potential misconduct, the agency confirmed, with people familiar with the matter saying the review centers on the communications office rather than protective details.
The Office of Professional Responsibility opened the review after concerns about possible unauthorized disclosures of sensitive information. Specific findings have not been made public.
Who is under review

The three employees are not sworn law-enforcement agents assigned to protection shifts, according to people briefed on the matter. One of the names circulating in reporting is a senior communications official who has served in the role since 2022.
The agency has declined to identify the individuals publicly while the process continues.
Context of scrutiny

The Secret Service has faced repeated questions about security planning and about how information about the president's movements and protective details is controlled. The current administration has emphasized leak investigations across several agencies.
Any finding that communications staff mishandled sensitive material would add to the pressure on an agency that has already undergone leadership and process reviews after prior security incidents.
What happens next
The Office of Professional Responsibility can recommend discipline ranging from counseling to removal. The timeline for a final decision was not disclosed.
Congressional committees that oversee the agency said they will seek a briefing once the internal process concludes.

keyTakeaways: Children with disabilities are overrepresented in foster care and have the worst outcomes.
They stay longer, move more often and face higher rates of institutionalization and death.
Advocates want better training, support payments and limits on residential placement.
articles.whyItMatters: Foster care is meant to protect children; the data show the system is least effective for those who need the most support.
articles.reportingNote: This report is based on public statements, court filings and contemporaneous coverage of the events described.
articles.title: Foster care often fails children with disabilities, investigation finds
articles.subtitle: Disabled kids make up a large share of foster placements and face the highest risks of long stays and poor outcomes
articles.excerpt: An examination of foster-care data and case records shows that children with disabilities remain in care longer, experience worse outcomes and are more likely to die in the system than their peers without disabilities.

content.text: Children with disabilities form one of the largest groups in the foster-care system and consistently record the worst outcomes, according to a review of national data and individual case histories.
They stay in care longer, move among placements more often and face higher rates of institutionalization and death than children without documented disabilities.
The numbers

Federal and state data show that disabled children are overrepresented in foster care relative to their share of the child population. Once in the system, they are less likely to exit to permanent family placements and more likely to age out without a permanent home.
Case reviews examined for this reporting described repeated placement breakdowns when caregivers lacked training or support for medical and behavioral needs.
System gaps

Child-welfare agencies often struggle to find foster homes equipped for complex medical care. Group homes and residential facilities fill the gap in many states, but those settings can limit family contact and educational stability.
Training for foster parents on disability-specific needs remains uneven, and coordination with Medicaid and special-education systems is frequently cited as a weak point by caseworkers.
What advocates want

Advocacy groups are pressing for higher support payments for specialized foster homes, mandatory disability training and stronger requirements that agencies exhaust family-based options before residential placement.

Several state legislatures have opened hearings on the issue this year after high-profile deaths of children with disabilities in care. Federal child-welfare officials said they are reviewing guidance on placement standards.
